title: Funky Focaccaia
description: It’s a Sunday afternoon, and golden light streams through the window as Lexie Smith tests recipes for Lalo — the forthcoming Chinatown restaurant from chef Gerardo Gonzalez (formerly of the buzzy coffee bar and luncheonette, El Rey), where she is the head baker. At the moment, three tres leches cakes chill in the fridge, squash stewed with kaffir lime leaves sits on the stove and Smith waxes poetic about the dough (a kabocha focaccia) pressed between her palms. This is typical: Smith baking bread and Georgia Hilmer photographing her, immersed in a friendship that almost never was — the kind of friendship that Vivian Gornick once described as one “in which people enliven one another.”
ingredients: ⅔ cups plus additional ¼ cup kabocha squash purée, *recipe below
1. Combine the flour, semolina and instant yeast in a bowl.
directions: In a separate bowl, break up ⅔ cup of the kabocha squash purée in the 1 ½ cups of water. Add the sugar.

Add the squash mixture into the flour mixture, and stir until combined, using your hand or a wooden spoon. Cover this for 20 minutes. (This resting time, before adding the salt, allows the gluten to begin to form.)

Combine the salt, miso paste and 1 tablespoon of water, and add to the dough. Using a wet hand, begin to pull the sides of the dough up and over the mass, keeping the mix in the bowl. Rotate the bowl, doing this movement (pulling out, up and over) on all sides, for about a minute. Each pull is called a “stretch and fold.” The mixture will be very wet and sticky! That’s a good sign.

Pour the olive oil around the edge of the bowl, along the perimeter of the dough, and rotate the dough so that you coat its bottom side with the oil. Cover and leave at room temperature for an hour and a half, performing four of the same stretch-and-fold movements (bring up each edge of the dough, one side at a time, folding it down over the rest of the dough like the sides of an envelope) every 30 minutes (three times total, during the hour and a half).
If you are pressed for time, you can skip the three stretch and folds and stick the dough in the fridge at this point, and let it rest there for at least 18 hours before baking.
Let the dough sit, covered, at room temperature for 45 to 60 minutes (it should be puffy and about doubled), then cover and refrigerate overnight or up to 48 hours.
When ready to bake, preheat the oven to 425 degrees.
Remove the dough from the fridge and prepare a sheet tray. Grease it generously with olive oil and cover it with parchment.

With a wet or greased hand, gently release the dough from the edges of the bowl and turn it out onto the sheet tray. Begin lightly pulling and pushing the dough toward the edges of the tray. I tend to spread this process out over about 15-30 minutes, letting the dough sit for a while in between pulls. (As the dough comes to room temperature, it becomes much easier to stretch. Be patient and you’ll retain more of those precious gas bubbles in the dough.)
Swirl the remaining ¼ cup kabocha purée around the surface, deflating the dough as little as possible. Cover. (I like to use another sheet tray, inverted on top.)
Proof the dough 60 to 90 minutes, or until puffy and quite wiggly. (It should wobble about like a melty marshmallow if you shake the pan.)

Bake for 20 to 30 minutes, or until golden brown and dry in the middle. (At this point, you can broil for about 20 seconds if you’d like a burnished top.) Remove it from the oven and brush generously with honey. Sprinkle with salt.
This bread will stay moist for a day or two, but is best eaten quickly and voraciously.
Kabocha Squash Purée
1 kabocha squash, cut in half
Oil, for the pan
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees.
Cut the squash in half and remove the seeds.
Place the cut side down on a greased sheet tray and roast for about 35 minutes, or until the top indents when touched. Remove from the oven and let cool.
Scoop out the flesh and blend it with a fork or food processor until smooth.
